Big Red, a huge, solidly built copper-chestnut draft mare with heavy white feathered legs, a wide white blaze, an enormous wild halo of curly copper mane and forelock, thin round wire-frame reading glasses, large gold hoop earrings in both ears, and a bold geometric-print blanket in burnt orange, deep plum, and mustard gold, with a confident side-eye and a smug red-lipped smirk. Standing tall in a barn aisle with one front hoof lifted and her head lowered in a long side-eyed stare at a tiny shaggy puppy sitting extremely straight and still in front of her, in a barn aisle with stall doors, halters on hooks, a wheelbarrow, a hay bale and a water bucket, with a small sign on the wall reading "Home Is The Barn". posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a huge copper-chestnut draft mare with round glasses, gold earrings and a geometric blanket, one hoof raised, giving a long side-eye to a tiny shaggy puppy sitting very straight in a barn aisle. Text at the top reads: The barn got a puppy. I gave it one look. It's been very polite ever since.
posts.caption: The new puppy arrived at the barn on a gray morning, and he'd clearly been told horses were large, soft, and friendly. He tested the first two. He trotted up to Red's stall with his tail going like a windshield wiper, and she lowered her head, slowly, until they were nose to nose. Nothing was said. He sat down. He's sat down most mornings since, at a respectful distance, like someone waiting outside the principal's office. The feed delivery guy asked who trained him. I told him nobody did. He just got the same briefing everyone else did.
posts.first: Red has never raised her voice at anyone, in any language she owns. She just moves her ears a certain way and the room reorganizes itself. I once watched a boarder rearrange an entire tack room because Red looked at it. I'm told that's not leadership. It looks a lot like it from here.

posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a round, fluffy dark brown Shetland pony with a cream forelock standing proudly next to a wheelbarrow he has pushed away from a wooden fence, looking innocent. Text at the top reads: Field report: the wheelbarrow was unattended. I've moved it four feet. The barn has not noticed.
posts.caption: I left the wheelbarrow outside the paddock gate for ninety seconds to grab a hoof pick. When I came back it was twelve feet away, parked neatly against the fence like it had always lived there. The handles were pointing at the house. Pudding stood next to it chewing a mouthful of hay and studying the middle distance. I moved it back and went to mix feed. By the time I came out again it had gone to the other fence. I've stopped being surprised, and I've started leaving it somewhere interesting. At this point we both have a routine.
posts.first: Pudding weighs about as much as the wheelbarrow, which I think he considers a fair fight. He's never once tipped it over. He just likes it where he's decided it goes. I've learned to check the barn every morning for where it's been moved to. Nobody will believe me, so I've stopped telling people.

posts.theme: the horse budget vs. the spouse
posts.quote: I drive a twelve-year-old truck so the trailer can have new tires. The horse has never looked at either.
posts.first: My husband asked why I'm still driving the truck with the cracked dashboard. I told him the trailer needs new brakes first. He gave me a look, then went outside to check the trailer. The horse has a blanket for every temperature and I own a coat I bought in college. It's all fine.

posts.caption: Somebody framed the old show photos last month and hung them in the tack room, in order, by year. Most of them are the real winners, shiny and braided, with the ribbons already pinned. Right in the middle is the Old Timer in 2012, standing at a slight angle, wearing a rosette that says 'Participant.' Somebody wrote a card for it and taped it up with duct tape. It's crooked. It's also the only frame in the room people stop at to talk. He walked past it twice yesterday, very slowly, lip hanging, and I'd swear he stopped to read it. He hasn't mentioned it.
posts.first: I put that photo up myself, with a nail left over from the fence. Everyone else had a trophy to hang. He had a face that has never once looked worried about anything. I figured that counts for something at his age. It looks right there, between the shelves and the old saddle soap.

posts.caption: Every month the barn splits into two camps, and neither one will admit it. The show crowd spends the night before braiding, packing, and eating granola bars in the tack room. By morning there are four trailers idling in the lot and everyone looks slightly haunted. Meanwhile Homebody has a bucket of warm mash and a quilt on the stall door. I walk past her on my way out to the trailers. She doesn't even open her eyes. Somewhere around mile twelve I always think about turning around. She was asleep when I got back, in exactly the same position.
posts.first: I've never managed to talk her into one show, and I've tried peppermints, a new halter, and once a very sincere speech. She watched me the whole time and went back to her hay. I think she's right more often than I admit. I came home with a seventh-place ribbon. She had the quilt.

posts.caption: The tack shop owner knows my name, my horse's name, and which scented products I'll be asking for next. I buy detangler in a size that should come with a warning. There are four bottles under the sink, a tub in the trailer, and one on the wash rack shelf with a rubber band around the cap. Last week the Diva sniffed the bottle, turned her head, and walked out of the wash rack. I held it up to my own nose. It smells like a hospital hallway. I went back to the shop and bought lavender. She came right back and let me finish her forelock.
posts.first: She has a very particular way of telling me I've failed. She doesn't spook or fuss. She just stands there with her chin up, and her ears say everything. I've known people with less range. It's cheaper to buy the lavender. It always has been.
